content: 1. The practice of antenatal care is strongly recommended for the prevention of pre-eclampsia, especially in pregnant women who are at a higher risk of developing hypertension. This recommendation aligns with WHO guidelines and is supported by moderate-quality evidence. 2. All lactating women diagnosed with active tuberculosis (TB) should receive iron, folic acid, and other essential vitamins and minerals as per the United Nations Multiple Micronutrient Preparation guidelines. This supplementation is intended to meet their maternal micronutrient needs, although the evidence supporting this recommendation is of very low quality. 3. In settings where contact tracing is implemented, household contacts of individuals with active TB should undergo nutritional screening and assessment as part of the contact investigation process. If malnutrition is identified, it should be managed in accordance with WHO recommendations, despite the evidence being of very low quality. 4. Nutritional assessment is a critical prerequisite for providing appropriate nutritional care. 5. There is no evidence to suggest that the nutritional management of severe acute malnutrition should differ between individuals with active TB and those without active TB. 6. Similarly, there is no evidence to recommend a different approach to the nutritional management of severe acute malnutrition in children with active TB compared to those without active TB. 7. Nutritional monitoring should be intensified, and nutritional support should be initiated earlier (preferably before the first two months of TB treatment are completed) if the patient’s nutritional indicators approach the threshold for severe acute malnutrition. 8. There is no evidence to suggest that the nutritional management of moderate undernutrition in children under five years of age with active TB should differ from that of children without active TB. 9. Efforts should be made to ensure that TB patients receive the recommended intake of micronutrients, ideally through food or fortified foods. If this is not feasible, micronutrient supplementation at the recommended nutrient intake level is warranted. 10. There is insufficient evidence to recommend that antenatal supplementation of calcium, iron, and folic acid should differ for pregnant women with active TB compared to those without TB. However, given the improved maternal and birth outcomes observed in pregnant and lactating women with HIV who take multiple micronutrient supplements, it is reasonable to consider similar benefits for pregnant women with TB. 11. If pregnant or lactating women with moderate undernutrition are receiving fortified supplementary food products, the micronutrient content of these products must be considered when prescribing additional multiple micronutrient supplements to avoid over-supplementation. 12. Screening for malnutrition, particularly in children under five years of age, is recommended during all healthcare encounters, including TB contact investigations. 13. The dissemination of WHO guidelines will be facilitated through electronic media, including slide presentations, CD-ROMs, and online platforms such as the WHO nutrition website, the WHO Global TB Programme website, and the e-Library of Evidence for Nutrition Actions (eLENA). These platforms will provide access to guidelines, systematic reviews, and complementary resources. 14. WHO will collaborate with international partners, including ministries of health, universities, and non-governmental organizations, to promote the adoption and implementation of these guidelines through workshops and other initiatives. 15. The guidelines should be adapted to the specific context of each Member State, taking into account available resources, existing policies, and delivery platforms. Ideally, these recommendations should be integrated into comprehensive TB care and support programs. 16. Monitoring and evaluation plans with appropriate indicators are encouraged at all stages of guideline implementation to assess their adoption and effectiveness. 17. The guideline will be reviewed in 2020, and if new evidence becomes available, a review group will evaluate the findings and revise the recommendations as necessary. WHO welcomes suggestions for additional questions to be addressed during the review process.
